pages.title: School canteen roster template — shifts, jobs and rules
pages.metaDescription: A school canteen roster template with real shift times, how many volunteers each day needs, the jobs to name, and the food safety rules by state.
pages.lede: The tuckshop roster is usually built by the person already cooking, which is why it falls over. Here is a canteen day hour by hour, the shift shapes that fill, and the rules that change at the state border.
pages.bodyHtml:
The canteen is not run by the school

In most Australian government schools the canteen belongs to the parent body, not the school — the P&C in state schools, the P&F in most Catholic and independent ones, and in Victoria the school council, an elected board of parents, staff and community members. The school provides the premises; the body operating the canteen is the employer, carries the legal responsibility and keeps the profit. That decides who builds the roster and who answers for it when nobody turns up on Thursday.

The staffing model is close to universal: one paid person plus rostered volunteers. That person is the tuckshop convenor in Queensland, canteen manager elsewhere, employed by the parent body rather than the department. They do menu, ordering, food safety, cash and supervision; volunteers do prep, bagging and counter under their direction.

Do not make the convenor build the roster

Rostering defaults to the convenor, so the person cooking is also the person texting at 8pm to fill Friday. Schools that run well split it off: a named volunteer roster coordinator who is a parent, with their own email address, so canteen questions and roster questions stop landing in one inbox.

A canteen day, hour by hour

A primary canteen day in the shape schools publish it.

TimeWhat happensShift
9.10amArrive, sign in at the officeMorning
9.15amOpen up, print and collate online orders by class, warmer onMorning
10.00amMorning tea food, start lunch prepMorning
11.20amServe recessMorning
11.40amWash up, hand overBoth — overlap
11.50amLoad warmer, prepare lunchAfternoon
12.40pmBag hot items, cutlery in, pack class basketsAfternoon
1.10pmClasses collect basketsAfternoon
1.20pmServe at the counterAfternoon
1.50pmClose up, clean downAfternoon
2.00pmSign outAfternoon

Offer three options: all day 9.10am–2.00pm, morning 9.10–11.50am, afternoon 11.40am–2.00pm. All day is cleaner and worth asking for first, because a split costs a handover mid-prep. Offer the split anyway, because it is what fills — and keep the ten minutes of overlap at 11.40, the only reason the afternoon volunteer knows what is in the warmer.

Two other shapes are worth stealing. Some primaries add a bagging shift, 12.30–2.30pm: short, low-skill, high-volume, and the easiest slot in the term to fill for a nervous first-timer. Secondary canteens run roughly 8.30am to 2.15pm on three to four volunteers; their break times often differ by day, so write the real recess and lunch time on each dated row, not in the header.

Count the slots before you promise anything

An Australian term runs nine to eleven weeks. A three-day canteen with two shifts a day is about 60 filled slots; a five-day secondary canteen needing four volunteers is closer to 200. Put that total at the top of the sheet.

  • Small primary, one to three days: convenor plus two volunteers a day.
  • Medium primary, five days: convenor plus two to three a day.
  • Secondary, five days: one or two paid managers plus three to four a day.
  • In every case a named reserve list. Not "ring around" — names.

Three days a week is normal, and far easier to staff than a five-day roster full of holes.

Name the jobs, including the one that is not a shift

"Canteen help 9–2" tells a new volunteer nothing. The real jobs: order collation, food prep, bagging and basket packing, counter at recess, counter at lunch, restocking fridges, EFTPOS and student cards, wash-up and clean-down. Online pre-ordering created the collation job and front-loaded the day, which is why the first shift now begins before the bell rather than after it.

Add a laundry line. Tea towels and aprons washed at home is a real rostered job, and the one thing to offer a parent who cannot attend at all. Put the perks on the roster too: free lunch on shift, tea and coffee, expenses reimbursed with a receipt.

The column everyone leaves off

Sign in and sign out. Volunteers sign in at the office or scan a QR code, and that record is what the school and your parent body's volunteer insurer will ask for if someone is injured or a child protection question arises later.

Use the notes column for canteen-specific things. Hair tied back or a net. No rings, bracelets or long nails on the prep bench. Where the anaphylaxis plan and first aid kit live, because a canteen handles allergens all day. And the one that matters most: anyone who has had vomiting or diarrhoea stays home — canteens commonly ask for 48 hours clear, and under the Food Standards Code a food handler with symptoms that may indicate a foodborne illness must not handle food.

Food rules: who actually decides

Canteen food rules vary by state and territory, and a school canteen is treated differently again from a one-off fundraising stall. Within a state it depends on what you sell, whether it is eaten straight after cooking, and whether you are a non-profit. That combination is why advice from another state — or from a club two suburbs over — is unreliable, and why this page will not tell you what applies to you. Getting it wrong runs both ways: groups buy certification they never needed, and groups skip an obligation they had.

The people who can actually answer it:

  • Your local council's environmental health officer. They handle notification, permits and inspection, and they will take a phone call from a volunteer committee. Ring before you print a roster, not after.
  • Your state food authority — the NSW Food Authority in NSW, Queensland Health in Queensland, and the equivalent in each other state and territory.
  • Food Standards Australia New Zealand publishes the national Food Standards Code and specific guidance for charities and community groups.
  • Your own parent body or committee. The P&C, P&F, school council or club committee usually holds the insurance and very often already has a standing answer from last year.

Two things hold everywhere. The food you sell has to be safe and suitable, and the people handling it need skills and knowledge appropriate to what they are doing. Everything past that is local, and worth ten minutes on the phone.

Put the term on one link

The .xlsx and .csv above run weeks down and shifts across, with sign-in, notes and a laundry line. Or paste the shifts into the volunteer roster: one link for the class group, full shifts close themselves, print or export at the end. Free, no signup. For the fete, the sizzle and the working bee, see the roster templates overview.

faq.q: How do you make a school canteen roster?
faq.a: Set the shifts first, then find the names. Build a grid of weeks down and shift slots across for the whole term, give every job a real title instead of writing "canteen help", add a sign-in column and a notes column, and put the total slot count at the top. Then hand the roster to a parent coordinator rather than to the paid convenor, who already has a job.

faq.q: How many volunteers does a school canteen need?
faq.a: A small primary open one to three days a week runs on the paid convenor plus two volunteers a day, roughly one per shift. A medium primary open five days needs two to three a day. A secondary canteen needs three to four a day alongside one or two paid managers. Keep a named reserve list in every case, not a vague plan to ring around.

faq.q: How long should a canteen volunteer shift be?
faq.a: An all-day shift of about 9am to 2pm is the cleanest, because splitting the day means handing over in the middle of lunch prep. Most schools offer the split anyway, since it is what fills: a morning of about two and a half hours, an afternoon of about the same, and ten minutes of overlap for the handover. Shorter works too, and a two-hour bagging shift in the middle of the day is usually the easiest slot in the term to fill.

faq.q: Do school canteen volunteers need a working with children check?
faq.a: It depends on the state and on who the volunteer is. Most states exempt a parent volunteering at their own child's school, but the exemption is drawn differently in each jurisdiction, and a grandparent or community volunteer may not be covered by it. Ask the school office and your state screening body rather than relying on advice written for another state.

faq.q: Does a school canteen need a food safety supervisor?
faq.a: Sometimes, and it turns on what the canteen actually does rather than on it being a canteen. The requirement depends on the kind of food handled — unpackaged, ready-to-eat and potentially hazardous food is treated differently from packaged snacks — and it differs by state and by whether the school is government, Catholic or independent. Ring your council's environmental health officer and your state food authority before anyone buys training. It is a short call, and assuming wrongly is expensive in both directions: groups pay for certification they never needed, and groups skip an obligation they had.

In most Australian government schools the parent body runs it, not the school — the parents and citizens association in state schools, parents and friends in most Catholic and independent schools. Victoria differs: the canteen sits under the school council, an elected board of parents, staff and community members. Either way the school provides the premises, and the operating body employs the convenor, carries the legal responsibility and keeps the profit.

pages.title: School fete roster template — shifts and headcounts
pages.metaDescription: A school fete roster that fills: one-hour shifts, how many people each stall needs, setup and pack-down crews, and a free template to download.
pages.lede: A one-day fete needs a couple of hundred sign-up slots, a named convenor on every stall line, and somebody thinking about pack-down months before the day. Here is the structure Australian schools use, and the shifts that never fill.
pages.bodyHtml:
A fete roster has two levels. Most templates have one.

Most Australian school fetes are not rostered from one desk. A fete convenor sits above a layer of stall convenors, one per stall, each recruiting and rostering their own volunteers. The convenor owns the shape of the roster and the empty slots. The stall convenor owns the names in it.

Build the sheet that way or it will not get used. Every line needs a named stall convenor and a mobile beside it: the job on the Thursday before is to ring fourteen coordinators, not two hundred parents.

Give each class a stall

The model that works is one stall per class or year level — Year 1 on drinks, Year 5 filling show bags — with the class parent rep as stall convenor. That turns an anonymous ask into a peer ask, which is what fills a fete.

One-hour shifts

One or two hours, with two and a half as the outer limit, and one hour converts best. Give parents the reasoning verbatim: shifts are cut small so you can still enjoy the fete with your own kids, or work a shift around sport or a party. Ask for a floor, not a range — at least one hour per family.

A roster you can copy

A 10am–3pm Saturday fete at a mid-sized primary school. Bump-in, setup, pack-down and the working bee are single blocks signed up to once; everything else is hourly.

Stall or jobHoursPer shiftSlots
Bump-in: marquees, mark out the ovalFri 4–7pm88
Setup crew7–10am1212
Gate and wristbands9am–3pm212
BBQ (five through the 12–2pm rush)9am–3pm426
Cake stall9am–3pm318
Trash and treasure9am–3pm424
Drinks and slushies10am–3pm315
Devonshire tea10am–3pm315
Rides and wristband check10am–3pm315
Face painting10am–3pm315
Games and lucky dip10am–3pm210
Silent auction and raffle10am–3pm210
Floaters and rubbish run10am–3pm210
Fete HQ9am–4pm214
Pack down, during close2.30–4pm1010
Pack down, after close4–6pm88
Oval working beeSun 9–11am88

That is 230 sign-up slots across the weekend, from twelve staffed lines plus the crews at either end. A twenty-stall fete runs past 350. Which is why the answer to "how many volunteers do we need" is hundreds, and why you need a count, not a feeling. The .xlsx and .csv version adds filled and vacant columns and a running total.

Sizing your own stalls: BBQ four to five, never fewer than three — one cooking, one serving, one on money, and money off food. Drinks, cake and Devonshire tea three to four. Trash and treasure four — one of them does nothing but tidy the tables. Games two, face painting three, gate two, HQ two continuously.

The lines nobody puts on the roster

  • Fete HQ. One staffed stall as the hub — spare rosters, first aid, lost children, lost property, sunscreen. Its own line, from before gates until the last stall cashes up.
  • Floaters. A named reserve pool for the midday peak and no-shows. Two an hour, and all get used.
  • Convenor hours are not shift hours. Stall convenors arrive hours before gates and stay through pack-down. Give them their own row and roster their break by name, or they will not take one.
  • The day's decisions need owners. Who calls wet weather and by when, who holds the keys, who counts out and collects the floats, who marshals every vehicle off the oval before gates.

Setup and pack-down are where it falls over

Look at almost any school's public fete sheet the week before: setup and the food stalls full, the after-close pack-up and the Sunday cleanup carrying nearly all the vacancies. Nobody wants to carry trestle tables to a shed in the dark.

Opening those shifts first and asking individually helps; the fix that moves the numbers is structural. Split pack-down in two. A during-close shift from 2.30pm strikes the quiet stalls while the fete is still running, in daylight; an after-close shift takes the marquees and the heavy gear. Ninety minutes each, with an end time in the ask. A twilight fete makes the split compulsory: undivided, it lands after bedtime and never fills.

Food and permits: who actually decides

Fete food rules vary by state and often by council. Within a state it depends on what you sell, whether it is eaten straight after cooking, and whether you are a non-profit. That combination is why advice from another state — or from a club two suburbs over — is unreliable, and why this page will not tell you what applies to you. Getting it wrong runs both ways: groups buy certification they never needed, and groups skip an obligation they had.

The people who can actually answer it:

  • Your local council's environmental health officer. They handle notification, permits and inspection, and they will take a phone call from a volunteer committee. Ring before you print a roster, not after.
  • Your state food authority — the NSW Food Authority in NSW, Queensland Health in Queensland, and the equivalent in each other state and territory.
  • Food Standards Australia New Zealand publishes the national Food Standards Code and specific guidance for charities and community groups.
  • Your own parent body or committee. The P&C, P&F, school council or club committee usually holds the insurance and very often already has a standing answer from last year.

Two things hold everywhere. The food you sell has to be safe and suitable, and the people handling it need skills and knowledge appropriate to what they are doing. Everything past that is local, and worth ten minutes on the phone.

The habit almost no school has

Give every stall convenor a folder holding what is known about that stall — suppliers, quantities, last year's helpers, what sold. It comes back updated after the fete, and the wrap-up happens a fortnight later while people still remember which shift had nobody on it.

Put it online

The table above pastes straight into the free volunteer roster: set the shifts, share one link per class group, and let parents put their own names down while full shifts close themselves. No signup, and it prints for the HQ table. The roster templates page has shorter blocks for the canteen and the sizzle.

faq.q: How many volunteers do you need for a school fete?
faq.a: Count slots, not people. A 10am–3pm fete with a dozen staffed lines comes to about 230 sign-up slots once bump-in, setup, pack-down and the Sunday working bee are counted, and a twenty-stall fete runs past 350. A smaller number of families cover that, most doing one to three hours each.

faq.q: How long should a school fete volunteer shift be?
faq.a: One or two hours, with two and a half as the outer limit, and one hour fills fastest. Short shifts let parents still walk around the fete with their own kids or work around sport and parties, which is the reason they say yes. Ask for at least one hour per family rather than offering a range.

faq.q: Who organises the volunteers for a school fete?
faq.a: Two people, not one. The fete convenor owns the master roster and the empty slots. A stall convenor for each stall recruits and rosters that stall's volunteers and reports back. Allocating one stall per class, with the class parent rep as stall convenor, is the usual way to fill it. Build the roster one to two months out and send every helper their details in the last fortnight.

faq.q: Do you need a food licence for a school fete stall?
faq.a: It depends on your state, usually on your council, and on what the stall sells — food cooked and eaten straight away is generally treated differently from food held hot or cold for hours. Non-profit fundraising is often treated more lightly than a commercial stall, but often is not always and the detail varies. Your council's environmental health officer is the one who decides, and your P&C or P&F has very likely asked them before.

faq.q: Do fete volunteers need a Working with Children Check?
faq.a: Ask the school, because the rules differ by state. A parent volunteering in an activity their own child takes part in is generally exempt in NSW and Victoria, but the exemptions are narrower than people assume and a school or P&C can require a check anyway. Sort it out well before the day rather than at the gate.

faq.q: How do you get the pack-down shifts to fill?
faq.a: Split it in two. A during-close shift from about 2.30pm strikes the quiet stalls in daylight while the fete is still running; an after-close shift takes the marquees and heavy gear. Ninety minutes each, with the end time stated in the ask. Open those shifts before the daytime ones, ask people individually, feed the crew, and put whatever is left on a separate Sunday working bee.

pages.title: Sausage sizzle roster — shifts, roles and ages
pages.metaDescription: A Bunnings sausage sizzle roster: four shifts, how many people each one needs, the seven jobs, who is allowed to cook, and the deadlines.
pages.lede: One BBQ, one gazebo and a very long Saturday. Here is a full-day roster you can copy, how many bodies each shift needs, who is allowed near the grill, and the deadlines that cancel your date before you ever get there.
pages.bodyHtml:
How many people you actually need

The figure most groups quote is sixteen — four shifts of four. It is also two too many at 8am and two short at lunchtime, which is why the template above is weighted to the middle of the day instead.

A realistic full-day minimum is 12 to 14 people plus a coordinator, weighted towards the middle of the day. Trade does not build to a neat noon peak either: a hardware car park fills from about 10.30am, so the shift to overstaff is the one starting at 10.

A full-day roster you can copy

WhenSlotPeopleWhat they do
All dayBBQ Captain17.30am–5pm. Not rostered on the grill
7.30–8amBump-in4Unload, gazebo, sandbags, plate hot, onions on
8–10amShift 131 cook, 1 bread and onions, 1 money
10am–12pmShift 2 — peak starts here52 cook, 2 bread and serving, 1 money
12–2pmShift 352 cook, 2 bread and serving, 1 money
2–4pmShift 431 cook, 1 bread, 1 money and drinks
10am–3pmRestock runner1Has a car. Ice, stock, emergency bread run
4–5pmPack-down4Degrease the pad, bag rubbish, cash up

That is 26 slot-fills, which 14 to 16 people cover once several take two shifts. Overlap changeovers by fifteen minutes, and put your two best people on 10–12 rather than 8–10.

The seven jobs

  • BBQ Captain (Bunnings' term; some groups say coordinator) — the one role the pack asks you to nominate. On site the whole time, runs the cleans, reports the expense and fundraising totals at the end of the day. Do not also roster them on the tongs.
  • Cook — one to two people, 18 or over. The job people burn out on fastest, so rotate it even within a shift.
  • Bread and onions — onion on the bread first, sausage on top, wrap, pass. Bunnings suggests that order because cooked onion on concrete is a slip hazard. This is the bottleneck at peak, not the grill.
  • Serving — takes the order, calls it to the grill, hands it over.
  • Money — float, tin, and card or QR payments. The pack is explicit that money is handled by people who are not cooking or handling food. If you use Bunnings' mobile payments, the captain registers the group first.
  • Restock runner — keeps raw product covered and below 5°C, and does the shops run if you are heading for a sell-out.
  • Cleaner — the pack asks for the BBQ area to be cleaned at least three times during the day. Put a name and a time against each one, or none of them happen.

Who is allowed to do what

This one breaks scout, cadet and junior sport rosters, where the obvious volunteers are teenagers. Nobody 12 or under has a role at the BBQ, including standing behind it. 13 to 17 can handle money, take orders and serve, but cannot cook or operate equipment. Only 18 and over cook, and gas bottles are connected and changed by a Bunnings team member only. So every shift needs an adult on the grill, however many willing fifteen-year-olds you have.

A car park sizzle is not usually child-related work under the state Working with Children Check schemes, but the schemes differ and your own club or school policy may still require a check.

The sell-out rule that breaks rosters

The pack asks you to be operational through the prime selling period, and that window varies — recent packs state 8am to 3pm as a minimum, older store packs 9am to 4pm. Read yours, because this rule is pinned to that finish time: if you sell out of sausages or bread before it, you are required to buy more and keep serving until it. Hence a named runner with a car, rather than a job the cook absorbs at 11.40am.

The paperwork gate

  • Store packs ask for the signed confirmation form and your council food permit, where one is issued, to reach the Activities Organiser four weeks before the date. One pack is blunt about what follows: if both are not in by three weeks prior, the date is cancelled and issued to another group.
  • You need a current public liability certificate of currency. $10 million is the usual minimum and some stores ask for $20 million, so take the figure from your own pack.
  • Popular metro stores are booked months ahead, sometimes a year. Book first, roster later.
  • Fourteen days' notice to cancel.

Food rules: who actually decides

Rules for a fundraising barbecue vary by state and by council. Within a state it depends on what you sell, whether it is eaten straight after cooking, and whether you are a non-profit. That combination is why advice from another state — or from a club two suburbs over — is unreliable, and why this page will not tell you what applies to you. Getting it wrong runs both ways: groups buy certification they never needed, and groups skip an obligation they had.

The people who can actually answer it:

  • Your local council's environmental health officer. They handle notification, permits and inspection, and they will take a phone call from a volunteer committee. Ring before you print a roster, not after.
  • Your state food authority — the NSW Food Authority in NSW, Queensland Health in Queensland, and the equivalent in each other state and territory.
  • Food Standards Australia New Zealand publishes the national Food Standards Code and specific guidance for charities and community groups.
  • Your own parent body or committee. The P&C, P&F, school council or club committee usually holds the insurance and very often already has a standing answer from last year.

Two things hold everywhere. The food you sell has to be safe and suitable, and the people handling it need skills and knowledge appropriate to what they are doing. Everything past that is local, and worth ten minutes on the phone.

What goes wrong

It is mostly the ends of the day, not the middle. The 2–4 shift evaporates at 3.55 and three people do a pack-down built for six, so name pack-down as its own slot with its own people. It is a real job: the pad has to be degreased, and all rubbish goes home in someone's car rather than into a Bunnings bin.

The rest repeats everywhere: the three cleans have nobody's name against them, so they happen once; drinks get under-ordered; and the captain ends up on the tongs by 10.30, leaving nobody to run handovers or keep the expense total the end-of-day report asks for.

Put it on a sign-up sheet

The rows above paste straight into the volunteer roster: set the shifts, share one link, and full shifts close themselves, so you do not end up with four cooks at 8am and nobody at half eleven.

faq.q: How many volunteers do you need for a sausage sizzle?
faq.a: Twelve to fourteen people plus a coordinator is a workable full day, and sixteen is the figure most groups plan around. Weight them towards the middle: three at 8am, five from 10am, five through 12–2pm, three in the afternoon, plus separate crews for bump-in and pack-down and a restock runner with a car.

faq.q: What time does a Bunnings sausage sizzle start and finish?
faq.a: The pack asks you to be operational throughout the prime selling period, and the stated window varies by store and by pack version — recent packs say 8am to 3pm as a minimum, older ones say 9am to 4pm. Check the pack for your store, then add about half an hour of bump-in and an hour of pack-down, which makes it a nine or ten hour day for the coordinator.

faq.q: Can teenagers help at a Bunnings sausage sizzle?
faq.a: Not on the grill. Bunnings' pack says nobody aged 12 or under has a role at the BBQ, including standing behind it, and 13 to 17 year olds can handle money, take orders and serve food but cannot cook or operate equipment. Only people 18 and over cook, and gas bottles are connected and changed by a Bunnings team member. Check your own club or school policy on Working with Children Checks for whoever supervises them.

faq.q: Do you need a food safety certificate to run a sausage sizzle?
faq.a: Ring your council — that is the honest answer, and it takes five minutes. Fundraising barbecues are frequently treated more lightly than a commercial food stall, but the rules vary by state and by what you sell, and the venue may add requirements of its own on top. Whatever the answer, the food still has to be safe and whoever is on the tongs still needs to know what they are doing.

faq.q: What happens if you sell out of sausages before the finish time?
faq.a: You are required to buy more and keep serving until the finish time stated in your pack. That is why the roster needs a named restock runner with a car from mid-morning, rather than sending a cook away from the grill at 11.40am.

faq.q: How far ahead do you need to book?
faq.a: Apply to your store's Activities Organiser well in advance — popular metro stores are booked months out and sometimes a year. Once you have a date, store packs ask for the signed confirmation form and your council food permit four weeks before, and at least one pack states that a date is cancelled and issued to another group if they are not in three weeks prior. Cancelling needs fourteen days' notice.
